content: When studies were analyzed collectively, significant heterogeneity was observed in the results. Meta-regression analysis, conducted to determine whether specific variables influenced the effectiveness of pre-exposure prophylaxis (PrEP) in reducing the risk of HIV acquisition, identified adherence as a critical moderating factor. Stratifying studies by adherence levels (high, moderate, and low) substantially reduced heterogeneity within these subgroups, indicating that differences in adherence levels largely explain the variability between studies. PrEP was most effective in the high-adherence group, defined as greater than 70% drug detection, with all studies in this group reporting adherence levels of 80% or higher. In studies with moderate adherence (41–70% drug detection), PrEP significantly reduced the risk of HIV acquisition. However, in studies with low adherence (40% or lower drug detection), PrEP showed no effect in reducing HIV infection risk. Safety data from ten randomized controlled trials comparing PrEP with placebo revealed that experiencing at least one adverse event during follow-up was common among participants in all trials. However, the rates of adverse events did not differ between the PrEP and placebo groups. Similarly, no differences were observed across subgroups, including mode of HIV acquisition, adherence, sex, drug regimen, drug dosing, or age. Eleven trials also reported on grade 3 or 4 adverse events, and no statistical differences were found between PrEP and placebo groups or across subgroup analyses. Several studies noted subclinical declines in renal function and bone mineral density among PrEP users. These changes did not result in clinical events and were not progressive over time. Drug-resistant HIV infections were rare, occurring in approximately 0.1% of PrEP users, primarily among individuals acutely infected with HIV at the time of PrEP initiation. The proportion of drug-resistant HIV infections did not differ between the PrEP and placebo groups, and mathematical modeling suggests that drug resistance from antiretroviral therapy (ART) far exceeds that from PrEP. No evidence indicated that PrEP led to risk compensation behaviors, such as reduced condom use or increased numbers of sexual partners. PrEP did not appear to affect the effectiveness of hormonal contraception, although two studies observed trends toward higher pregnancy rates among oral contraceptive users who also took PrEP. This relationship became nonsignificant after adjusting for confounders. Oral PrEP was not associated with increased adverse pregnancy-related events among women taking PrEP during early pregnancy. However, more data are needed on interactions between PrEP and hormone therapy used by transgender populations. PrEP was evaluated for its effectiveness in preventing HIV infection within the context of comprehensive HIV prevention packages, including regular HIV testing, counseling, condom provision, and screening and treatment for sexually transmitted infections. Cost-effectiveness analyses suggest that PrEP may be cost-saving in settings with an HIV incidence greater than 3 per 100 person-years. In lower-incidence settings, PrEP may still be cost-effective, particularly when targeted to populations at substantial risk of HIV acquisition. Studies have shown that higher PrEP uptake and adherence are associated with greater cost-effectiveness, particularly among men who have sex with men in concentrated epidemics. Equitable access to PrEP can contribute to improved health outcomes by preventing HIV infection and sustaining the health of users and their sexual partners. Expanding PrEP recommendations beyond narrowly defined groups, such as men who have sex with men and serodiscordant couples, can promote equitable access and reduce future treatment costs by preventing HIV in high-incidence populations. PrEP acceptability has been reported across diverse populations, including women, serodiscordant couples, female sex workers, young women, people who inject drugs, transgender individuals, and men who have sex with men. Implementation of PrEP has been shown to be feasible in various trial settings and demonstration projects. However, significant barriers to uptake and adherence have been identified, particularly among women in placebo-controlled trials. Open-label studies have demonstrated higher adherence among women. Demonstration projects in Botswana, South Africa, Thailand, and the United States confirm that protective levels of adherence are achievable for most PrEP users, although challenges remain in achieving high adherence among young people. Implementation considerations include addressing legal and social barriers, ensuring PrEP does not displace other effective HIV prevention interventions, and promoting PrEP as a positive choice alongside other prevention strategies. Stigma, a driver of HIV, could be reduced or exacerbated depending on how PrEP is implemented. Comprehensive implementation guidance from the World Health Organization (WHO) is expected to address practical aspects such as human resource utilization, laboratory monitoring, pharmacy services, drug procurement, counseling, and community engagement. Healthcare providers should be trained to explore sexual and injection risk behaviors with patients, help them assess their HIV risk, and discuss prevention options, including PrEP. Providers must offer respectful and inclusive services, develop strong patient-provider relationships, and address barriers to healthcare engagement and adherence. Services should be tailored to meet the needs of young people, especially young women and key populations, and involve community participation in program development and implementation. Community-based organizations can play a significant role in reaching high-risk populations, providing information about PrEP availability, and linking individuals to healthcare services. HIV testing is required before initiating PrEP and regularly during its use. Renal function should be monitored before starting PrEP and periodically during use, with creatinine testing preferred. Hepatitis B testing is also recommended, as PrEP medications are active against hepatitis B. PrEP should always be provided alongside other HIV prevention options, with community-based organizations supporting outreach and education efforts.
